title: Production Readiness Best Practices 🛡️
description: Make your workloads production‑grade with requests, limits, PDBs, and affinity.

slides.title: What Does 'Production‑Ready' Mean? 🎯
slides.content:
# It's more than just running

A production‑ready workload must:
- Be resilient to failures (node crashes, network splits)
- Not starve other applications
- Respect node constraints (zones, hardware)
- Stay available during voluntary disruptions (drains, scaling)

Kubernetes provides several features to achieve this: **requests/limits**, **PodDisruptionBudgets**, **affinity/anti‑affinity**, **tolerations**, and **topology spread constraints**.

slides.title: Setting Resource Requests & Limits (Revisited) 📏
slides.content:
## Non‑negotiable in production

Always set resource **requests** and **limits** for every container.
- **requests** guarantee resources and influence scheduling.
- **limits** prevent a runaway container from starving others.

Example:
```yaml
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: "200m"
    memory: "256Mi"
  limits:
    cpu: "500m"
    memory: "512Mi"
```

Without them, your Pod is **BestEffort** – the first to be killed under pressure.

quizData.question: What QoS class does a Pod get if every container has CPU and memory requests equal to limits?
quizData.explanation: Guaranteed QoS requires requests == limits for every container.

slides.title: PodDisruptionBudget (PDB) 🛡️
slides.content:
## Protect against voluntary disruptions

When you drain a node or perform a cluster upgrade, Pods are evicted. A PDB ensures a **minimum number or percentage** of Pods remain available.

```yaml
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: myapp-pdb
spec:
  minAvailable: 2          # or maxUnavailable: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: myapp
```

If only 3 replicas exist, you can't evict more than 1 at a time because `minAvailable: 2` must be respected.

quizData.question: A Deployment has 5 replicas. A PDB sets `minAvailable: 4`. How many Pods can be evicted simultaneously?
quizData.explanation: Only 1 Pod can be disrupted at a time to keep 4 available (5 - 1 = 4).

slides.title: Node Affinity & Pod Affinity/Anti‑Affinity 🧲
slides.content:
## Control where Pods land

- **nodeAffinity** – attract Pods to specific nodes (e.g., SSD nodes, GPU nodes).
- **podAffinity** – place Pods near other Pods (e.g., app and its cache).
- **podAntiAffinity** – spread Pods apart (e.g., avoid all replicas on the same node/zone).

Example: anti‑affinity to spread replicas across zones:
```yaml
affinity:
  podAntiAffinity:
    preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
    - weight: 100
      podAffinityTerm:
        labelSelector:
          matchLabels:
            app: frontend
        topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
```

slides.title: Full Pod Spec with Affinity
slides.codeSnippet:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
spec:
  affinity:
    podAntiAffinity:
      requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
      - labelSelector:
          matchLabels:
            app: frontend
        topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
    nodeAffinity:
      requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
        nodeSelectorTerms:
        - matchExpressions:
          - key: node-type
            operator: In
            values:
            - worker

slides.title: Taints and Tolerations 🧪
slides.content:
## Repel or allow specific Pods

- **Taint** on a node: "no Pods here unless they tolerate me".
- **Toleration** on a Pod: "I can handle that taint".

Useful to dedicate nodes (e.g., `CriticalAddonsOnly` taint on master nodes).

```yaml
tolerations:
- key: "node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane"
  operator: "Exists"
  effect: "NoSchedule"
```

This Pod can run on a control‑plane node.

quizData.question: What's the difference between a taint and node affinity?

options.text: Taints attract Pods, affinity repels them
Taints repel Pods, affinity attracts Pods

quizData.explanation: Taints let a node repel a set of Pods; tolerations are the Pod's permission to ignore them. Affinity/anti‑affinity attract or repel based on Pod/node labels.

slides.title: Topology Spread Constraints 🌍
slides.content:
## Even distribution across zones, nodes, etc.

```yaml
spec:
  topologySpreadConstraints:
  - maxSkew: 1
    topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
    whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
    labelSelector:
      matchLabels:
        app: myapp
```

Ensures Pods are spread so no zone has more than 1 Pod difference from the least loaded zone. Great for high availability.

slides.title: Production Checklist ✅
slides.content:
- Set resource requests/limits.
- Use PDBs for apps with >1 replica.
- Spread Pods across failure domains (zones/nodes).
- Use health probes (liveness, readiness, startup).
- Run as non‑root with SecurityContext.
- Enable NetworkPolicies.
- Monitor with Prometheus/Grafana.
